articles.title: Solving the Floating-Point Problem in Agentic Reasoning
articles.excerpt: Large Language Models (LLMs) are remarkably good at logic but fundamentally flawed at precision. When you ask an agent to multiply $1/2$ by $1/3$, it isn't performing division; it is predicting tokens…
articles.body: Large Language Models (LLMs) are remarkably good at logic but fundamentally flawed at precision. When you ask an agent to multiply $1/2$ by $1/3$, it isn't performing division; it is predicting tokens based on statistical patterns learned during training. For many tasks, this probabilistic approximation suffices. However, when we move toward specialized domains—engineering, finance, or scientific computation—that probabilistic nature becomes a liability. The failure mode is predictable: floating-point errors or subtle inaccuracies creep into the reasoning chain. In standard IEEE 754 arithmetic used by most programming environments, certain decimal expansions cannot be represented exactly, leading to rounding drift.

articles.title: Auditing Expiring and Unattended Credentials with Python
articles.excerpt: Local development servers, build runners, and staging machines frequently accumulate unattended secrets. Files containing TLS certificates, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), service account configurations, and S…
articles.body: Local development servers, build runners, and staging machines frequently accumulate unattended secrets. Files containing TLS certificates, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), service account configurations, and SSH private keys are written during maintenance or testing and then forgotten. Over time, these files create two distinct operational risks: Silent Expiration: Certificates and signed access tokens expire unexpectedly, breaking scripts, local proxies, and automated tasks. Hygiene Failures: Key pairs and API credentials sit unrotated for months, often stored with permissive file permissions that allow any user or local process on the host to read them.

The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

articles.body: LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13). After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour , sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall. "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour.

articles.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
articles.excerpt: Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?
articles.body: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
